chapter: Early recordings and arrival in New York
title: October 1937 vocal date and the 'Modern Svengali' press
summary: Songs from the date, 'Easy to Love' and 'Nice Work If You Can Get It', all chosen by Claude, plus the newspaper headline about her.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Okay. Let's move on to the 22nd of October 1937.
This was a vocal date, It's "Easy to Love", "The Folks Who Lived On The Hill."
Another song with a rather unusual structure and rather a traditional song by "Darling Nellie Gray" -- and It's "Nice Work If You Can Get It."

"Easy To Love" and "Nice Work If You Can Get It" did wind up on the DownBeat poll for the release of the week -- you know, that they ran it every week. And I think "Nice Work If You Can Get It" and "Easy To Love" both ran first and second, and second and first for about a month.
So I had gotten that far getting listed.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

And, of course, I always liked "The Folks Who Live On The Hill." And, of course, "Darling Nellie Gray" was more in keeping with the traditional style that he had established by doing the early "Loch Lomond" and "Annie Laurie" thing.
And these were all, of course, Claude Thornhill's selections, because he was my mentor.
In fact, while the news was getting around, Archer Winston who was a critic for one of the newspapers -- he hadn't really got into hearing Maxine Sullivan.
But I guess the news got around, and it was a very big spread in the paper -- I think it was the Telegraph.
It said "Modern Svengali Discovers Sepia (inaudible)." Twilby?
So that didn't hurt either. We made headlines then.
